turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Howzit, come on through. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, nothing much, doc. The knee's been a bit cheeky, that's all. I'm otherwise lekker.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cheeky how? Talk me through what it actually does.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right knee. Going down the stairs it niggles, and some nights it wakes me. Hardly a crisis, hey.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did you first notice it?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't pin a date on it. Last winter, or the one before. It sort of crept up and the months run together.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it swell, or give way under you, or lock so you can't straighten it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. It doesn't give way. It doesn't lock. I'm not an invalid.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Those nights it wakes you, how often is that really?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Two nights, maybe three in a week, if I've been on my feet. I turn over and it's fine. Not worth a fuss.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been using on it, or taking?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac gel from the chemist, rubbed on the knee morning and night. And now and then a diclofenac tablet from the pharmacy if the stairs have been cruel.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Strength of those tablets, and how many in a week?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I think they're the fifty milligram ones. I nearly said every day — no, not every day. I swallow one by mouth, maybe twice a week. No diary, it's not that serious.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tummy trouble from them? Heartburn, indigestion?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems at all. Cast iron.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Other medicines, the regular ones?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Enalapril for the blood pressure, ten milligrams every morning. Been on it for years. That's the lot.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's the blood pressure been, from your point of view?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): They said it was fine last visit. I don't have a machine at home. No drama.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone x-rayed this knee along the way?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, at the hospital. They said it was borderline. Not bad, not brilliant, and nobody wanted to operate.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was that x-ray, roughly?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really sure. Not this year. Could be three years, could be more. I chucked the paper.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the pain stop you doing the things you like?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I still do the garden, slowly. Shame, the neighbour fusses more than I do. It's a niggle.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Glad you're still out there.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Speaking of weekends, did you see the Proteas? My grandson was shouting at the TV the whole afternoon, under-eleven and already a commentator.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): He's keen, then.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Mad about it. Wants a new Gray-Nicolls bat and his mother said absolutely not. We watched until the last over.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): And did he stay over?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Every second weekend. Getting him home, the robots on the M1 were out, queue back to the petrol station. Forty minutes, and he recited the batting order twice. Lovely, exhausting.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): That traffic is no joke. The storm missed us as well, didn't it, and then soaked the far side.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Bone dry in my beds, drenched over there. He thought it was the funniest thing. Anyway.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's come back to the knee, if you don't mind. You said the stomach is happy with the diclofenac.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I told you, no stomach problems. Well, actually, I do get heartburn after supper, if there's a curry or a rich braai. A Rennie and it's gone. That's the food, not the pills. Nothing, really.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often does that heartburn show up?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Once or twice a week, maybe. I don't clock it. It's minor.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the Rennie, just when it comes?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, one by mouth, sometimes two if I have a second helping. Chewable. Then I'm right as rain.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can I ask about your weight? Stairs put a proper load through a knee.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, I've picked up a few kilos, I won't pretend otherwise. Since I stopped walking the dog. It's not heaps, and I'm not joining a diet club.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did those walks stop?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): The dog went, and I just... last year, or the year before. Couldn't give you the month. I still potter in the garden. That's enough exercise.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair. Hop on the bed and I'll look at the right knee. Shoes off is perfect.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): You won't find much. I'm telling you it's nothing.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bend and straighten... there's crepitus under my hand, no fluid in the joint, and it's not warm. Ligaments feel steady.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Steady. I said it was nothing.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): A little tender under the kneecap, and on the inner side. You did flinch, even while you're shrugging it off.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Only a little. I've had worse off a garden fork.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have a seat again. Thinking out loud, pain coming down stairs and at night can be ordinary wear and tear, osteoarthritis, or it can be the kneecap side, patellofemoral. That old film being called borderline would fit either. I'm not going to conclude which one it is today.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're not sure. That's fine. I didn't come for a grand label.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): We could send you for physiotherapy, or do a steroid injection into the joint if the gel isn't carrying you. I don't want to decide either of those today.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't book me a needle. Physio is a schlep too. Leave it.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave both open. I'd like you to ease off the diclofenac tablets by mouth, though. With the heartburn I'd rather you weren't taking them even twice a week. Keep the gel morning and night, that's kinder on you.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. I'll try. They're only for the bad days, but alright, I'll leave them.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): And those few kilos — even a small drop takes load off the knee on the stairs. Not a lecture. Just something that genuinely helps.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll think about the weekend boerewors. No promises, doc.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks. We'll see if the gel and a bit less weight are enough, and only then choose physio or the injection if we still need to.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks is fine. If it's still nothing I'll tell you it's still nothing.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the heartburn gets worse, or the knee suddenly swells or gives way, don't wait the six weeks. Come sooner, or go to casualties. Otherwise I'll see you then.

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
